editor_spans.body: The citation for Tyrone's new Lord-Lieutenant points out that he was District Commander in Omagh on the day of the 1998 bombing. It does not mention that the statutory Omagh Bombing Inquiry, set up in 2023 and chaired by Lord Turnbull, is still asking whether the attack could have been prevented, and that the conduct and intelligence of the RUC are central to that question. Appointing the officer who commanded that district as the Crown's representative while the inquiry is still sitting is a choice that families who doubt the official account may notice. The honours system treats long local service and contested history as separate things, but in Northern Ireland they rarely are.

Derby is not a new choice. It won the competition to host the Great British Railways headquarters in 2023, under the previous government and its 2021 rail plan. This week's news is only the building: work starts in 2027 and finishes in spring 2029. That puts nearly a decade between the plan to create GBR and the day its staff move in. The project has survived a change of government because 'one railway in public hands' appeals to both parties. The slow part is not the policy but turning it into an institution.

Two claims in the announcement deserve care. The fare freeze is a funding decision by the Treasury, and a privately franchised railway could have had one too, so it is not a result of public ownership as such. The more telling number is buried: fewer than 7% of rail workers are under 25. Up to 600 apprentices over four years is small against an ageing workforce that has built up over decades. The skills gap, more than who owns the railway, may decide whether GBR works.

The government's language on Ukraine is stronger than its numbers. In one week we got 'doubling down', 'go further and faster' and 'for as long as it takes'. What was actually new was a £45m missile package, of which £10m is being brought forward, set against £1.6bn already committed over four years. Ministers have been asked to 'draw up' sanctions, military and fiscal packages, which means they do not exist yet. Meanwhile the US has reached its own agreement with Russia, and the UK's response was careful: it 'fully supports US-led efforts'. London's real influence seems to lie in shaping what Washington agrees, not in its own deliveries.

The strongest reason London backs an energy ceasefire is a domestic one. The Prime Minister described it as the quickest way to get diesel back onto world markets, and the 9 October response pointed to energy prices and the cost of living. Ending Russian strikes on Ukraine's grid would also take pressure off British fuel prices. That shared interest makes the policy sturdier than an appeal to solidarity alone. It also means that if fuel prices ease by other means, the pressure to keep the ceasefire going may fade.

The most significant line in the Commons statement got the least attention: an offer to discuss 'the different options' for the UK's long-term relationship with the EU, with 'the British public' as 'the boss'. This moves away from the previous government's red lines on the single market, customs union and freedom of movement. 'The public will be the boss' is how politicians prepare the ground for a referendum without promising one. The 20 November summit on food standards, emissions trading and youth mobility is the first step. The statement's own figures show why the government is moving: £100m a year in lost Scottish salmon exports, banned seed potatoes and shellfish, and a possible 20% cut in Northern Ireland's wholesale energy costs. Ten years after the 2016 vote, the government now treats what Brexit costs in practice as the case for reopening it.

Burnham's offer to Holyrood takes his Greater Manchester mayoral model and applies it to Scotland, presented as a joint project. In practice it gives Westminster, through No10 North and the Scotland Office, a reason to deal directly with Scottish regions, and it casts the Scottish Government as the bottleneck: 'one of the most centralised devolved administrations in Europe'. Any SNP government will see this as going around Holyrood. Whatever happens to the offer, it moves the argument from 'Westminster vs Edinburgh' to 'Edinburgh vs Lanarkshire, Fife and the Highlands'. That shift is the lasting political point.
